paragraphs.heading: Listening for other minds
paragraphs.text: SETI, short for the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, is a broad set of scientific projects that try to detect signals, or any other evidence, of intelligent life beyond Earth. Researchers watch for electromagnetic radiation, look for optical signals, and study objects that could be artifacts made by others. Some projects work the other way round and send messages outward, such as NASA's Golden Record.

paragraphs.heading: Radio and the Martians
paragraphs.text: Modern SETI began in the early 20th century, once radio existed. Early in the 1900s, Guglielmo Marconi, David Peck Todd and Lord Kelvin all said they believed radio could be used to reach Martians, and Marconi claimed his stations had picked up possible signals from Mars. In August 1924, when Mars came nearer to Earth than at any time in the previous century, the United States promoted a National Radio Silence Day, with radios going quiet for five minutes on every hour. At the US Naval Observatory a receiver was carried 3 kilometres up in a dirigible, in a program led by Todd. William F. Friedman, the US Army's chief cryptographer, was assigned to translate any message from Mars.

paragraphs.heading: Project Ozma
paragraphs.text: In 1959 Philip Morrison and Giuseppe Cocconi wrote a paper that was the first to suggest searching the microwave part of the spectrum, and it proposed frequencies and a first list of targets. In 1960 the Cornell astronomer Frank Drake ran the first modern SETI experiment, called Project Ozma. He aimed a 26-metre radio telescope at Green Bank, West Virginia, at two stars, Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani. He listened near 1.420 gigahertz, a stretch of radio nicknamed the "water hole" because it lies close to the spectral lines of hydrogen and of the hydroxyl radical.

paragraphs.heading: The Wow! signal
paragraphs.text: Ohio State University approved and built a radio telescope known as Big Ear, which later ran the world's first continuous SETI program. On August 15, 1977, a volunteer named Jerry Ehman noticed an unusually strong signal picked up by this telescope. He circled the reading on a printout and scribbled "Wow!" in the margin. Some people regard this Wow! signal as the best candidate ever found for an artificial radio signal from outside Earth, yet later searches have never caught it again.

paragraphs.heading: Bigger plans, better receivers
paragraphs.text: In 1971 NASA paid for a study, involving Drake and Barney Oliver of Hewlett-Packard Laboratories among others, that proposed Project Cyclops: a ground-based array of 1,500 radio dishes with a price of US$10 billion. Cyclops was never built, but its report became the basis for much later SETI work. In the early 1980s the Harvard physicist Paul Horowitz proposed a design for a spectrum analyzer made just for hunting SETI transmissions. Older analyzers relied on banks of analog filters, which capped how many channels they could handle, while digital signal processing on integrated circuits could check far more. The result, a portable unit called Suitcase SETI with 131,000 narrow channels, went into use in 1983 on a 26-metre telescope at Oak Ridge Observatory in Massachusetts.

paragraphs.heading: The search today
paragraphs.text: In 2015 Stephen Hawking and Yuri Milner announced Breakthrough Listen, a 10-year, $100 million effort to detect signals from nearby stars. International work has gone on since the 1980s, including community-run projects such as SETI@home and Project Argus that help analyse data. Related research on unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP), for example the Galileo Project led by Avi Loeb, has also drawn fresh attention to SETI.

paragraphs.heading: Doubts and defenders
paragraphs.text: Decades of work have produced no confirmed evidence of intelligent aliens, and critics have called SETI overly hopeful. Some argue the whole effort is speculative and cannot be proven false. Supporters see it as an important step toward addressing the Fermi paradox and toward understanding possible extraterrestrial technosignatures. SETI is a respected scientific field built on rigorous methods and checkable data, yet the public often lumps it together with conspiracy theories and UFO research.
